assumptions: Source definition: f is expressed in metres, and converging/diverging focal signs are retained.
Application scope: paraxial optical focal power, with an unambiguous effective focal length and exterior-medium/wavelength conditions.

gaps: Add optical_power meaning and coherent 1/m (diopter alias D optional); add/use focal_length as proposed in b01. Do not bind energy-rate meanings to optical_power.

models.inverse_notes: Inverse f=1/P requires finite P!=0 and has one signed root; f/P signs agree. P=-20 inverse metres gives f=-0.05 m and forward substitution returns -20. P=12.5 gives f=0.08. P=0 denotes an infinite-focal-length boundary, not f=0; no finite root. This inverse is the same definition, not a new relationship.
limitations: Zero power is physically meaningful but needs infinite focal length, so cannot be obtained from a finite f in this serialization.
Not surface vergence, angular magnification, or radiant power in watts; a unit match alone does not identify them.

references.method: Published College Physics 2e Example 25.5 reports 12.5 D for 8.00 cm. Convert f to 0.0800 m, preserve power as 12.5 inverse metres. Tolerance 0.05 is half the source output's 0.1 D increment.

Published diverging-lens paragraph following Example 25.5 gives -5.00 cm and -20 D; keep -20 as expected. Tolerance 0.5 inverse metres is half the last displayed integer-D increment, not an estimate of actual lens uncertainty.

rejection_cases.reason: A zero focal length makes the defining reciprocal undefined.
Focal length is required in this view; an unspecified lens has no assumed power.

relationship.locator: University Physics 3 Eq. 2.23; College Physics 2e Eqs. 25.20-25.23
relationship.translation_notes: Keep source P and f. Use coherent 1/m for diopter: 1 D=1 m^-1, a unit name equality with factor one, not an extra physical coefficient. With f in metres the canonical expression is 1/f, not 100/f. The numerator 1 is dimensionless reciprocal arithmetic. Dimensions L^-1. Original f!=0 retained; a zero-power optical element has infinite focal length and cannot appear in this finite-f input view.

variables.context: Same paraxial lens or equivalent close-lens system, optical wavelength, material state and common exterior medium. Real-is-positive convention: f and P positive for converging optics, negative for diverging optics; lens reference plane and effective-focal-length definition must match.
variables.definition: Signed paraxial effective focal length of this lens or equivalent lens system in its specified exterior medium.
variables.domain: Finite nonzero, positive converging and negative diverging.

variables.context: Same paraxial lens or equivalent close-lens system, optical wavelength, material state and common exterior medium. Real-is-positive convention: f and P positive for converging optics, negative for diverging optics; lens reference plane and effective-focal-length definition must match.
variables.definition: Signed reciprocal effective focal length, in inverse metres (diopters); not radiant/mechanical/electrical power.
variables.domain: Finite nonzero for this finite-focal-length view; either sign.

assumptions: Source approximation: individual lens powers add when the lenses are sufficiently close; the record uses coaxial thin lenses in contact or optically negligible separation.

Application profile: powers use the same surrounding medium, wavelength and converging-positive convention; components remain thin and the complete stack has negligible thickness for the intended accuracy.

gaps: Add optical_power and coherent 1/m; family sum evaluation exists, but no family inverse runtime view is supported. Every actual component instance needs the common coaxial/contact/wavelength/medium context, not just a shared generic string.

models.inverse_notes: Automatic inverse views of family models are not supported. By hand, a selected component power equals P_total minus the sum of all other known component powers; every other component and the component count must be known, and common-context/thinness conditions retained. No denominator exclusion or sign branch. For total=8 and known components 10,-4, the remaining power is 2; substitution 10-4+2=8. A zero total with known +5 gives remaining -5, unique. If two or more components are unknown, infinitely many signed allocations yield the same total; a zero total alone does not identify individual powers.
limitations: Finite lens separations generally introduce cross terms, so merely specifying nearby lenses does not establish acceptable error.
No source error bound or empirical tolerance for nonzero separation is reported here; use is conditional on the thin/contact approximation.
The 256-element capacity does not authorize a physically thick 256-lens stack; the optical thinness condition still governs.

references.method: Independent synthetic paraxial ray reasoning: a parallel ray at height 0.001 m has slope changes -0.010,+0.004,-0.002 through three ideal contact elements, giving total slope -0.008. It crosses the axis after 0.125 m, whose reciprocal effective focal length is 8 inverse metres. This uses contact ray deflections and resulting focus rather than replaying sum(powers); tolerance covers exact synthetic arithmetic.

Limiting identity: equal opposite contact powers cancel every paraxial angular deflection at unchanged ray height. Parallel input stays parallel, so total power is zero; the system does not have focal length zero. Exact synthetic components, floating-point allowance only.
Definitional one-element limit: the only component is the whole system. Expected -4 inverse metres is independent of any multi-element arithmetic; exact synthetic power.

rejection_cases.reason: At least the component-power family must be supplied; no implicit zero-power system is assumed.

relationship.locator: University Physics 3 Eq. 2.25 and its closely-spaced qualification
relationship.translation_notes: Introduce powers as a bounded indexed family of the source component P values; P_total retains the source meaning. Coherent unit 1/m for every input/output, so summing dimensions L^-1 produces L^-1; no scale factors. Family capacity 256 is a format ceiling only. Source finite-spacing qualification is respected by the optical-contact/negligible-spacing application profile. Component powers are supplied, rather than inlining a chain of separate lens maker/focal relations. Zero total retains its legitimate afocal interpretation even though a separate finite-f reciprocal record cannot consume it.

variables.definition: Signed optical powers of the component thin lenses, each specified in the common exterior medium and at the common wavelength.

assumptions: Source assumption: paraxial reflection; ray heights much smaller than curvature radius and rays make small angles with the axis.
Source sign convention: concave R,f positive; convex R,f negative.

constants.meaning: Paraxial geometric factor from two equal focal-length segments in the radius; not a material constant.

gaps: Add signed_spherical_mirror_radius; reuse focal_length in the declared mirror context. m exists. An explicit sign adapter is needed before relating mirror radii to b02 signed refracting-surface radii.

models.inverse_notes: Inverse R=2*f has one root for any finite nonzero signed f, retaining the same mirror sign and paraxial conditions. f=-0.3 gives R=-0.6 and forward substitution gives -0.3. f=0 would imply R=0, outside the surface domain. The plane mirror requires the infinite-radius limit; no finite zero or additional branch represents it.
limitations: A finite-aperture spherical mirror has spherical aberration; this is not an exact all-ray focus condition.
The plane-mirror limit requires infinite R/f and is outside the finite scalar view; R=0 is not that limit.
Does not infer reflector area, collected energy or transmission.

references.method: Published Example 2.1(a) gives required f=40.0 cm and solves R=80.0 cm. Convert to metres and retain 0.400 m expected. Tolerance 0.0005 m is half the final 0.1 cm reporting step; only the optical portion of the example is used.

Published Example 2.2 reports R=-0.80 cm and f=-0.40 cm, preserved as -0.0080 m input and -0.0040 m expected. Half the 0.01 cm output reporting step is 0.00005 m. This is a rounded textbook inverse result, not a measured corneal calibration.

Independent synthetic paraxial reflection geometry for a convex surface: at ray height 0.001 m, normal tilt magnitude is 0.001/0.6=1/600 rad; reflection doubles the outgoing angular deviation to 1/300. Backward axis intercept is -0.001/(1/300)=-0.3 m. Synthetic ideal-paraxial data; tolerance covers decimal arithmetic.
references.provenance: https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-3/pages/2-2-spherical-mirrors# law-of-reflection and isosceles-triangle derivation preceding Eq. 2.2

rejection_cases.reason: Zero curvature radius does not define the paraxial finite-aperture spherical surface; it is not a plane mirror.

relationship.locator: University Physics 3 Eq. 2.2 and spherical-mirror sign convention
relationship.translation_notes: Retain f,R. R is a signed spherical-mirror radius: its sign is positive for concave and negative convex, unlike the refracting-surface radius convention in b02. The geometric divisor 2 comes from R=CF+FP and equal paraxial segments CF=FP; it is attributed in constants, not a fitted coefficient. L/1=L. All lengths in metres; no conversion multiplier. A plane mirror is R infinite, not R=0, and is outside finite inputs.

sources.evidence: Paraxial spherical-mirror focal length is half its signed curvature radius. Concave radius/focal length are positive, convex negative. Examples report (R,f)=(80.0 cm,40.0 cm) and (-0.80 cm,-0.40 cm).

Real-is-positive mirror convention: R and f positive for concave reflecting surface with real focus on incident side, negative for convex reflecting surface with virtual focus behind it. Do not use the opposite signed refracting-surface radius convention.
variables.definition: Signed radius of the spherical reflecting surface: positive concave, negative convex in the real-is-positive mirror convention.
variables.domain: Finite nonzero signed spherical radius; zero radius is no finite-aperture spherical mirror.

variables.context: Same paraxial spherical reflecting surface, axis and vertex reference. Real-is-positive mirror convention: R and f positive for concave reflecting surface with real focus on incident side, negative for convex reflecting surface with virtual focus behind it. assumptions: Source assumption: homogeneous isotropic medium, constant index along the specified ray segment.
Application profile: real positive phase index and forward nonnegative path length; no backward/signed tracing, complex attenuation index or anisotropic mode ambiguity.

gaps: Add optical_path_length and geometric_ray_path_length with distinct definitions, reuse phase_refractive_index. Units m and 1 exist. A compound-path aggregation may consume per-segment optical_path_length values, but no destination model is asserted here.

models.inverse_notes: Solve s=opl/n given opl>=0,n>0; unique nonnegative s. Solve n=opl/s given s>0,opl>0; unique positive n. Example opl=0.018 m,s=0.012 m gives n=1.5 and substitution restores 0.018. s=0,opl=0 leaves n undetermined; s=0 with opl>0 is inconsistent. opl=0 with n>0 uniquely implies s=0; do not impose s>0 on that inverse direction merely because the n solve needs it. No phase/group-delay inverse or anisotropic branch assessed.
limitations: For a nonuniform medium, the general path integral is not represented by one constant-index product; piecewise homogeneous optical lengths may be summed after each segment is computed.
OPL is not automatically a group-delay distance in a dispersive medium.
No phase, interference, diffraction, polarization or intensity model is included, even though the source discusses them.

references.method: Independent synthetic length measure: split a 12 mm uniform path into twelve 1 mm pieces. Each has 1.5 mm index-weighted length by the per-unit definition, giving eighteen millimetres in total, expected 0.018 m. This is a definitional/additive construction, not observed data; it checks the metre scale and nonunity coefficient. Tolerance covers exact synthetic decimal arithmetic.
Definitional identity: a vacuum segment is already the reference index-one path, so weighted and geometric lengths coincide. Synthetic 0.7 m; tolerance covers binary representation.
Zero-path limiting identity: coincident endpoints add no geometric or optical length, whatever the supplied positive index. This is not a claim about a zero-thickness physical lens.

rejection_cases.reason: A negative number is not the forward geometric arclength declared here; signed/backward tracing requires a different profile.
The medium's phase index is required and cannot be inferred from the path length.

relationship.locator: Ansys Optics What is a ray?, Amplitude, phase, and optical path: OPL=nt display
relationship.original_equation: OPL = n t (t is geometric distance, not time)
relationship.translation_notes: Rename source t to s because t in this article is a geometric lens-unit length, not elapsed time. Local opl is source OPL. Normalize s and opl to metres; n is dimensionless real positive phase index for this application profile. Dimensions 1*L=L. Optical path is distinct from geometric length even though both have length units; no speed or time is introduced. A zero-length segment is an admitted coincident-endpoint identity with zero optical path. Does not import the article's phase or diffraction equations.

sources.evidence: For a ray segment in homogeneous isotropic material the article defines optical path length as refractive index times geometric distance. A multi-medium ray's complete optical path sums the segment optical lengths. Only that geometric definition is used here.
